video_title: If UPI Is Free, Who Pays for It? | PhonePe, Razorpay & NPCI | WTF is Payments?
transcript: [Nikhil] The entire history of money has been one move, repeating. Money keeps getting lighter. It started as grain and cattle, something you grew or herded, or could physically run out of. Then, it became gold coins stamped by kings, so heavy with meaning that entire empires ran on the weight of it. Gold became paper, a promise, instead of the metal itself. Paper became plastic. And, in India, money became a sound. The next move for money might be the strangest one yet. Something I've asked so many people, but nobody knows clearly. If you were to ask an AI data centre person, he would probably say money is moving to energy. I don't know which way this will play out. Maybe there is a business to be built around betting what that change might be. Grain, gold, paper, plastic, stablecoin, things on the blockchain, and I'm sure it'll change tomorrow as well. Today, I'm talking to people who built the last version of this story, the people who turned money into a sound. Sohini is the ED of growth at NPCI, the organisation behind UPI. Harshil Mathur is the co-founder of Razorpay. Sameer Nigam is the CEO and co-founder of PhonePe. We'll get into their journeys, the wins, the losses, the years nobody was watching, and where the next move in this history gets made. Because if you want to understand how India spends, or how to build the next big thing in this country, there's no one better place to teach you than the three people who will be sitting across from me today. Should we start by drawing a diagram of the different kind of payments and map out how it began? Okay, thank you guys for coming and doing this. So, let's begin with introductions, and who would like to go first? Okay, I can go first. We'll start from the very beginning. So, I was born in Rajasthan, went to this lovely school in Jaipur, school and college both, actually, initially, in Jaipur, and then went, did my MBA at this exclusive college for defence personnel and their dependents only, Symbiosis in Pune. Joined a bank, Axis Bank, spent... spent about 18 years doing lots of interesting non-core bank kind of things. So, all of payments, all of digital, all new initiatives. So, you know, I think that was kind of the grounding. Then went and-- Oh, before that, actually, in college, met my boyfriend and then now husband, my husband for more than 25 years now. -Then went to-- -What's his name? Siddesh. Yeah. Is he a regulator? -[Sohini] No. -[laughter] More the moderator than the regulator, I think. But yeah, then I worked in Western Union, the money transfer company that took me across the shores, spent some time learning about a lot of different countries and the way businesses are run there. And almost like, full circle, came back last year... to come and lead growth for NPCI, which actually can be a little interesting because... How do you grow a company which is already doing, like, roughly a billion transactions a day? So, I'm still figuring that one out. Is it a government posting or is it like private sector? You know, that's a very interesting question. Almost everybody asked me that question when I was joining as well to say, "So, are you going to be working for the government?" My father wanted to know if I'll get a white Ambassador with the Ashoka Stambh on it or not. Unfortunately, no. So, this was formed by RBI and IBA. So, it's set up as a not-for-profit. And yes, there is an element of us working-- Because it's a digital public infrastructure, so we work closely with the government and the regulator. It's a Section 8 company, right? -Yes, it's set up as a not-for-profit. -Who funds it? So it was set up with an initial funding of 100 crores. -By? -By ten banks. And now, actually, after that, it has generated enough surplus because it's not profit and it's not returned back to the shareholders, but all of the growth and the investments and the tech and the infrastructure and everything has been kind of self-funded. -Do Section 8 companies have shareholders? -Yes. And who are your shareholders? -Banks, fintechs, yes. -[Nikhil] You are? So, initially, we had to invite people to be our shareholders. Why? Because, initially, when it was just an idea, and it was just like-- It started with saying the ATM transactions, like the NFS, which was the National Financial Switch, which was set up to say that is some part which will be done by this company. -So, it's a long journey, where-- -But, as a shareholder, does Sameer make money on NPCI shares if you do well? So, because we don't return any money back to shareholders in the form of dividend, the surplus just goes into, like, the corpus for investments. -Right. -So, but at this point of time, -we are not set up like that. -Can you change like that? Can you change from Section 8? -I know OpenAI did something like this. -Yeah, yeah. So, technically, can you and "can you" can you are different questions, Nikhil. -So, technically, maybe yes. -Would you like to, if you had to choose? I think it's a "point in time" question. -At what point in time? -Now? Now, maybe not, because now I think there is still a lot that needs to be done. And to take the... to take the focus away on saying, "Hey, your main aim is to return value back to the shareholders," will take it away from the purpose. What if it becomes half the aim? -What if it becomes? -Half the aim. Like, a part of the money is returned back to shareholders. I don't think there are any half measures there, Nikhil. Like, the mandate that we have at this point of time, I think it's important that we continue on that journey. I'm also asking you for myself, 'cause I'm in fintech. I'm thinking, "How much can I pull your leg? Will you rap me tomorrow if I say something?" -[laughter] -Are you the regulator? -The reason both of us are a little quiet. -Are you independent? -Yeah? -Come on, Harshil. No, but, you know, I have to answer this one because... We are not the regulator. You will get us in trouble by calling us the regulator. There's only one regulator, and that's the Reserve Bank of India. But you know, this happens in stock broking, where NSE is not a regulator, but they can act like a regulator. -Ah. -They have some power to be a regulator. They're almost like a private regulator. They're not Section 8. -They're very different from you. -[Sohini] Yeah. But you must have some power that the Razorpay and PhonePe guys do not have, right? Um... I want to look at their reactions first. No, but you know what? The way we operate-- -Okay... -[laughter] No, so the way we operate is through steering committees, like, you know, so every decision-- And it's very difficult because of the fact that now, at this stage, there are lots of differing... priorities, right, for the different constituents of even the steering committee. Initially, obviously, everybody was at the same size, same scale, same... Now, there are lots of pushes and pulls, but most of our decisions still get taken through a steering committee framework. If Harshil does something that really bothers you, like something bad, what can you do to him, either directly or, like, you know, through someone? -I'll give you an example. -Okay. If there is-- If, on a particular app, frauds increase, okay, because they haven't put in some controls, so, our way of penalising will be, you cannot onboard new customers anymore now, -till you go back and fix it. -That's a big penalty. No, but that's important because that, like-- Unless you go fix this, you cannot onboard new customers. It's not like, hey, penalty in the sense of, like, you know, financial penalty or anything. -This is a financial penalty only... -It is. ...if you can't onboard new guys. Yeah, but it's important that you go and fix what needs to be fixed. So it will have to be something of the order of your risk controls not being adequate. I think that's needed as a-- For security of the system. -'Cause finally-- -You will obviously have to say that. [laughter] If someone else is doing it, it'll affect me, I will also suffer. Right. But accountability, finally, is to the Indian public. It's the vulnerable who get defrauded. So we have to-- -we have to take care of that. -Okay. But you have done a lot across the spectrum of payments, in a way. What did the Axis Bank experience teach you? A lot of things, actually. Are banks becoming irrelevant? I've thought about this. To a certain extent, regulation is harder for them... to compete on a fair queue. Like, if I'm trying to borrow money on the back of, say, private equity, a bank is not allowed to lend. I have to go to an NBFC. Like that, in many departments, banks are over-regulated or regulated so much more than a fintech player that that less regulation itself becomes a moat for fintech players. There are many ways to look at that, Nikhil, because, see, why are-- See, this is-- You're taking one part of it in isolation, because if you look at it, banks have to be regulated because the NBFC is not... taking deposits from the customers. The fact that you're taking the public money and then you're doing XYZ with it, you have to be regulated. So, you know, yes, this you can say that's the moat for the fintechs, but then there are other moats for the banks, and banks have got to leverage and work on their moats to be able to do that. Just cost of capital, no? Do they have any other moat? No, there's cost of capital, there's also-- And even in that, like, what, 2%-3% lower? It's not just about 2%-3% lower. The fact that they have that access which others do not have, like why did payment banks fail? -Again, regulation, I think. -No. Payment banks failed because you couldn't take... -Above one lakh, right? -You couldn't lend, you couldn't, yeah, your deposit taking capacity-- But there was regulation, no? -You can't take money above 1,00,000? -Exactly. -So, that model failed. -No, that's retail. You can take corporate deposits, those are larger, but you can't lend, or you can't... I think it's the same balancing act. If you can't take public money, you can't do this, then you are less regulated as well. If you take public money, you're also more regulated, so it's a-- Are payments banks dead? Like, I know Airtel is still running it. -Airtel is the one doing decent. -Airtel is the one, India Post is the one that is-- India Post wanted to exit or something like that was going on. Yeah, I think India Post because, again, of the structural-- That's the only one that is alive now, and there's Airtel. -Airtel is doing well. -And Jio Payments Bank which, again, I'm not sure whether they're not-- Even the SFB licencing didn't work out, right, small finance bank? Actually, that's worked out better. That's worked out better. -Why is that? -[Harshil] They can lend. Because they started with lending. They could lend. But they have some rule that you have to allocate... -Priority sector, yeah. -...30-40%. Banks also have priority sector rules, they have just higher priority sector rules. If you take a Slice today, that's an SMB. If you take a Shivalik, that's an SMB. So, priority sector is, I think-- Especially in the digital age, getting access to tier-2 and beyond customers is not hard. Is there a carrot at the end of that road that SFB will become universal? You can apply and convert. [overlapping conversations] -Is that what incentivises SFBs the most? -Yeah, yeah. I think that should be the-- Again, this is-- Especially the easier part in becoming a universal bank. Regulation also follows. You know, for a while we were trying to get a banking licence and when I spoke to the regulator, they showed me that Niti Aayog had made a white paper asking for a digital-only banking licence. [Sohini] Okay. It was a recommendation to the government that it should happen, but the people in the government then pointed to payments bank and said, "This is meant to be that, but this is not that." Yeah, this is not that. This is not that. See... Payment or digital only banks, so, this, you have to look at global examples. Many of the countries have done it and failed, like, even Southeast Asia, they tried to create this Grab Bank, GXS, etcetera. If you look at Revolut, which is like a... -roaring success, killing it, right? -Killing it! -[Harshil] Nubank. -Nubank, they got it right, but lots of other countries tried to go this route only, "We will give out licences." All of Southeast Asia, actually, "We will give out licences." And then they have all these conditions, then they make it a process, then there are three or four conglomerates which will come together. That never works out, no, so... But isn't there a case to be made to have digital only bank in India? There should be, there should be, yeah. -[Sameer] Lots. -That one, I think-- -You are kind of the regulator. -[laughter] You should tell, people will listen to you. Yeah. Right now, we find it difficult to make Harshil and Sameer listen to us. Just saying. [Sameer] Retail banking, we all know. So, he is admitting that, selectively, he'll listen to us... Okay. Harshil, would you like to go next? Sure, sure, and by the way, I didn't know you're from Jaipur. -I'm from Jaipur as well. -Wow, where? I grew up in Malviya Nagar, schooling from Seedling. -Okay, so I went to MGD. -Oh, nice. I mean, we spoke so many times, we didn't know we are both from Jaipur. I was born in Jaipur, grew up in an average middle class family in Jaipur. Dad worked in a bank. -Manager? -Banker. He was a clerk, actually. He became a manager by the time he retired. In SBI. And then, so, went to college in IIT Roorkee, was always-- Same, my dad. Became a manager around when he retired. Canara Bank. Yeah, close to two years before he retired. -Yeah, Canara Bank. -Yeah. Because you typically get posted out of the city -when you become a manager, so you-- -You get transferred every three, four years, right? Yeah, so that's why he avoided till retirement, till my schooling was done and all of that. So, yeah, went to IIT Roorkee, was always very deeply interested in computers from, like, school days, used to code stuff on the side. But unfortunately, I didn't make the rank in IIT, so I got into mechanical. Didn't know what to do with mechanical, had zero interest in it. You must have got like 99.2% instead of five, right? Yeah, I mean rank, rank. So I got a 1800 rank. You need to get under 1000 to get computer science. [Nikhil] Right. So, took mechanical, had zero interest in it. So, started forming this group of people who were interested in coding but couldn't do coding in their school time. And so we created a software group called Software Development Section. The group survives even today. So that's... So that was a college group where people would basically spend their time coding and building stuff. That was my first idea of building a startup of sort because I had to raise funding for it. And I can tell you, like, raising money from a government institution was harder than-- much harder than raising money from VCs. Because even if you do raise money, spending it is very hard. -You have to do tenders and all that. -So it is fairly painful. But that was my first experience of raising money. Now it's become hard to raise money from VC? I mean, raising money from VC is-- I'm saying it's much easier compared to raising from government institutions. Like, it is extremely hard. Every single rupee is audited, every single rupee is controlled. So it takes a lot of effort. You know one thing I didn't know about you? Black belt in karate. -[laughter] -Doesn't look like it. If I was in a fight, I wouldn't think, "Call Harshil." I don't know if it is a good thing or a bad thing. -No? -It sounds like a bad thing. -Would you have guessed? -I'm not messing with him. [laughter] I was a black belt. I actually got a silver in nationals. -[Sohini] Really? -What are you saying? Yeah. So, yeah, so then... So, at that point, I did learn how to, like, build stuff and things together. Met Shashank, my co-founder. So, graduated from college, again, because of mechanical got placed in Schlumberger, which is an oil company. Shashank was in Microsoft. And both of us talked that, "Man, I don't have any interest in this job. Let's try to build something of our own." So, while we were in our respective jobs, we used to keep building stuff on the side, side projects, like, doing something or the other for fun, like college. And for one of those things, we wanted to accept payments on that. So, we were building a social crowdfunding platform. Like, Facebook was very popular. So, we wanted a way for people to raise money for causes. More a side project, not a-- I would not say it was a startup. And for that, like, building the product was easy. The hardest problem was accepting payments. So we tried all the banks and the large payment players and all that and found it is extremely-- almost impossible to get through. It took us a couple of months. Even after we got an approval, the tech interface was extremely poor. Like, it was built for, I don't know, I'll say old school '90s world. And it felt like maybe we had a bad experience. So I started going to these-- Facebook was the most popular social media, so I would go to Bangalore startups, Pune startups, these Facebook groups, say, like, "How do you accept payments?" And everyone said, "Yeah, it's easier to accept cash, so just start accepting cash." I mean, Flipkart was, of course, the largest payment-- like, largest e-commerce company. COD was extremely popular. So, these are the five ways you can accept cash. Just go and accept in cash. That hit my techie brain hard. Like, the point of most tech is democratisation, right? So, like, Internet gives everyone access to information, social media gives everyone a voice. So, it didn't make sense to me that something digital is harder to do than something physical. So, it should be increasing access. So I started searching, researching online, "Why is that complicated? Why is it so painful?" And honestly, I couldn't find any real reasons for it. So, me and Shashank started speaking, "Should we try something in this?" And we had no idea of finance. My only exposure to finance was my dad used to work in a bank. -But beyond that, nothing else. -Which is no exposure. Which is no exposure. So, I remember I just walked into a bank branch next to my home on one of my off days, next to my home in Jaipur, and said, "I want to build." I learnt that payment gateway is a term used. So I said, like, "I want to build a payment gateway," and the guy said, "Do you want a payment gateway? I can give you one." "No, I said I want to build my payment gateway. How do I go about it?" And, of course, the guy had no idea. Nobody goes to a bank branch in Jaipur and says, "I want to start a payment gateway." So, connected me to somebody in Delhi. I spoke to that guy, explained what I want to do. He said, "No, you can't do it. Like, just get out of it." So, because, like, two 24 year, 25 year olds out of college, with no finance background, you don't just go and start a payment gateway. -Went to the next guy and so on. -Harshil is very proper, no? -Right? -Why proper? In the sense? Like, I have never seen you khul ke. -You know what I mean? -You have seen me khul ke, by the way. -When? -At your home. -Not fully khul ke, half khul ke. -Maybe you were also khul ke then. [laughter] -[Sohini] So you don't remember. -So you don't remember. -No, no, but I've not seen you like... -Unleash. Unleashed. Like, Sameer is always unleashed. -Yeah, that's true. -Yeah. -Okay. -Yeah. Why do you hold yourself back? I think it's a matter of company and time. Company, meaning, in front of me you tend to be like this? [stuttering] You have seen me. -[laughter] -There was a company then. Who was there? There were a lot of folks from Bangalore, the ecosystem and all that, so yeah, you have. There is an alter-ego. -There is a Fight Club moment. -Yeah. I feel the quietest ones are the craziest ones. [Sohini] Hmm. -[Nikhil] You know? -I kind of agree. -Yeah. -Right? [Nikhil] Yeah. Everybody has a mental picture going on now of Harshil doing crazy things. -I didn't agree because of me. -[Nikhil] I have one. -Now I have karate-crazy Harshil. -Karate. -Karate, pickleball and drinking. -I don't know what else will come out now. [laughter] -That's interesting, Harshil. -You tell me. What shall I say? I am-- Whatever you wish to say. I was born in Bombay into a naval family. My dad was in the Navy, small town guy from UP, went to IIT, naval architect. So, born here. I started my schooling in Germany. -Will you have some coffee? Black? -Absolutely. Yes, sir. -Coffee? Black? -Black is good. -Coffee, yeah. -Coffee is always welcome. Germany, yes. So that was interesting. I was, like, a four-year-old kid. I learnt German before I learnt English. -You still know it? -Very poorly. I understand more than I can speak. But the coolest part was, I think, at age 7, when they completed India's first submarine, we all got, families got invited. We sat in a submarine at age 7. I'll never forget that in my life. [Sohini] Wow. It's the only thing I remember, except German, besides German chocolates. Those are the two things I took away. Moved back to Delhi, spent about six years there. And then, at 13, I moved back as a teenager, moved back to Bombay. And it was the best damn place and time to move back. Early '90s was fun times in Bombay. We partied a lot. Met my co-founder now, Rahul, in undergrad. -Yeah, I think the best party. -There's no denial. So I was basically-- I was the serious one, Rahul was the party animal, if you've met him. No, I'm just kidding. He was through and through the brightest kid I knew in school. And I figured, "If I do something someday, I'll do it with this person." But dropped ship from there, went to the US. And, you know, at that time, I wanted a startup. I had no business skills and no background in my family, not even the banking part of it. Moved there, joined a startup after grad school in LA. The LA part was, I think, easy after Bombay. Partied hard, worked hard, worked in a startup, learnt the ropes, met my now wife there. When? What year? -We met on more than one road trip... -If you don't remember, it's okay. -...in 1999, 2000, 2001. -No worries. I'll make a reel about this and send it to your wife. No, no, there's many walks of shame there, don't worry. -They're captured in Polaroid. -Yeah? We partied out there, but virtually, yeah, it was really good fun. A company called ShopZilla, it was comparison shopping. I actually love just consumer Internet companies. This is the early days of the Internet. One of maybe first 10 clients that Google ever had, and Google broke after I had started working, and Yahoo and all these guys, so that entire hub, that was really good fun. Left in 2007, went to Wharton for a couple of years, started up my first venture. You can tell the Bombay and LA blood was there. So started a digital music company, went about aggregating music from all the Indian labels, and all the global labels, just basically, partying with all the studios. We never made any money. It had nothing to do with digital payments. They just never paid. [Sohini and Sameer chuckling] So, sales and collections are two different things. But we sold it to Flipkart in 2011. I moved to Bangalore, spent four amazing years there. -So, we saw their-- -Can I ask you a question? -Yeah. -In 2007-09, people went abroad, did MBA, a lot came back. Why are they not coming back now? I think, by '07... people, the first crop of people post-liberalisation who'd gone, had seen enough, and there was a view that India's digital moment will come. I think, right now, the macros are not in favour. I'm talking to a lot of young kids. My son's turning 18. They don't want to come back, no? I don't think that-- The middle-class aspirants don't want to be here. And I think it's sad. And, um, I mean, on a serious matter, I think it bothers me because I came back. I've had a great run, you've had a great run. But I think-- When you say macros are bad, what do you mean? I think there's a population of people that has grown up in the Insta world, in the YouTube world, that has seen what's possible out there. And they're seeing governments and markets opening up. And they're seeing... governments not sort of getting in the way of just unleashing animal instincts. And I think we are at an inflection point. We're at a weird inflection point. I feel like India is still living in the past. And I think we have 300-400 million people who want to just look ahead. They're not really married to the past. When I talk to my kids, I mean, these are Gen Zs, my daughter's 13. You see what's happening around socially right now with unrest. They don't really care if we are 5,000 years old, 3,000 years old. They want to move in traffic. They want to get to some place. They want to move ahead. -And they should, damn it. -Even we think like that, no? Yeah, they should. That's what I'm saying. So, I'm rebellious enough, but it frustrates me. I've seen better. But I made a conscious choice. I remind myself every day. I made a conscious choice to move back. I think a lot of people who are seeing things are not making that choice today. And it's a little sad. Yeah. Hope is what keeps the world going, isn't it? But will it change? You think it'll change? I think it will change if... If we change our relationship societally with government, I think it'll change. Say again? If we change our expectation and relationship with governments, and I think, for India, we may be 30, 40, 50 years away. The vote bank of India. There's 500 million people who depend on the government machinery to keep things moving. There's 500 million of us who are now saying, "You're slowing us down." So, India is this contrast of realities. Where are we at as a country? We're 75 years old. We're a young democracy. And, in many ways, it's like one of the most amazing social experiments on the planet. We are borrowing a lot of pride or glory from the past to feel energised, I mean, especially with this government. But, in general, how do you feel good if you are coming out of 700-800 years of servitude and poverty? You have to look as far back as you can, or if you don't have that history, then you just look forward. The US never had a history to worry about, they only look forward. They have-- They can't talk about the past. Before George Washington, they have no idea what was there. The era before George Washington, the third chapter of my history would be done. Meaning, it was irrelevant. -250 years is nothing. -But I heard Alex Karp, the Palantir person, say a very interesting thing. For a civilisation to do well, it's important that we believe that we are special. Yeah. Americans inherently believe that they deserve more because they are special, even if they don't go back to history. This is a bad example, but Hitler, the Aryan race, whoever thought they were better than the others and they deserve more, they ended up doing better, from the economic lens. So, Indians looking back 2,000 years ago and thinking we are better, -it's possibly not a bad thing. -No, I'm saying it's a good thing. It's just, unfortunately, because you have to borrow from the past, the need to build hammer and tongs, like, fast and improve ourselves, I'm not seeing that come. And maybe that will come in the next, let's say, 10 years, because we will-- people will demand better roads and people will demand better infrastructure. There's just... a breaking point. -Bombay had it 30 years ago. -But that might not be connected, right? Japan is a good example of a country that looks a lot to its past and is still going forward, right? So, you can continue to look at your past. -I have a different take on this. -It's way smaller, man, way less complex. I spent a lot of time in China. Like, I was there for a month, two months ago. They have one unique thing that, whatever you know, Communist Party, this, that, and the other. In their factories, when I was going through the manufacturing line, there used to be these things written on the board, which are their core values. Self-criticism is everywhere. The problem with us is if we don't acknowledge what is not working, how can you fix it? I think, partly where you're right is when you're saying we look back at the past and say we are great, it's also making us not look at the problems of today. -We're not acknowledging them. -We're deflecting. I think they can go hand in hand. You can continue to look at your past, but also see what went wrong. -The second part we are missing. -Yeah. We are not acknowledging that this is not working. Right now, if you see anywhere, everybody is saying, "India is great, India is great." No, but the great and the pride, no, I'll tell you one of the things. You can have a lot of pride in your past, but if you look at, say, China or Japan or any other country right now, leave the US out, US is like a different... The pride has to be in the pride of the quality of your work, right? Like, quality of work at every level, and we don't see that, right? This whole jugaadu mindset, which has been celebrated so often, I think this part of our problem is this... like you said, we deflect or we are not looking at-- So that the pride is slightly misplaced in the sense that-- "Okay, fine, it's okay to--" You want to shut your eyes to the problems of today, so you say, "Oh, 5,000 years ago we invented AI or Wi-Fi," or whatever else we want to talk about, but we will not like it if someone is doing like the most basic work. We see any of the places which get inaugurated or something, there is no sense of-- UPI is a great example. I was there on ground zero and I promise you this, for all the tom-toming we do, there was maybe 20 people responsible for it. I'm not talking about enabling NPCI, I'm talking about building UPI. And a lot of them are sitting in Bangalore. And it's the paradigms that shaped UPI. It's going mobile first, it's about building tech that's interoperable, it's about building APIs that people can build on. -Those are technology choices. -[Sohini] Yeah. There was no brouhaha, there was no chest thumping, none of that. It followed so quickly that today, and you know this and I know this, let's be frank, right? You can't take a step forward without taking at least 0.75 back every single time because we have this incredible habit as a country that we almost invite regulation and government into places that has no goddamn business into.
